facts.t: Appears in 1.96% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive (465 paintings, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 229).
In our 23,781-painting archive it is more common than 72% of the named colors.
Peaks in the 1900s: found in 1.5% of the 1,674 paintings we have from then (25 paintings). Against the same museums' baseline that is 1.5x the expected rate.
Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color (39% of the 229 paintings, by lightness rank within each painting, so varnish cannot fake it).
Most devoted painter: Paul Cezanne, in 8 of 50 works here (6.7x the baseline of the museums those works come from; as photographed 4.6x; n=8).

First seen in our archive in 1435 (commons-Q4009968, by Fra Angelico); the third-earliest painting is 1445, and the latest 1950 (378 dated paintings, at least 2% of the canvas, as photographed). The archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first.
Shares canvases with Deep Slate-Olive and Artichoke Green more than chance (lift 9.7 and 6.5; n=33 and 30).
In printed English the word peaks in the 2000s and rose fastest in the 1920s (Google Books, all senses of the word, so a color name that is also an object or a place can mislead).

That is 662 years before the name's earliest record in our sources (1912): the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of the pigment or dye.
